section_summary: This section assembles State and War Department intelligence reports on Japanese nationalist propaganda in Hawaii, especially Dr. Teikichi Sato’s 1935 lecture tour, together with reports and duplicated enclosures concerning allegations made by Korean activist Kilsoo Han under the pseudonym W. K. Lyhan. The later pages contain an anti-Japanese memorandum and a broad clipping file on Japanese-language schools, cultural festivals, citizenship and loyalty, propaganda, shipping, trade, statehood, and Japanese communities in Hawaii and Canada. The section concludes with a newspaper list of University of Hawaii degree recipients.

subfiles.title: Assessment of Dr. Teikichi Sato’s Hawaiian activities
subfiles.about: Assesses Sato as a Japanese nationalist propagandist whose activities appear relatively harmless.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum characterizes Dr. Teikichi Sato’s Hawaiian speeches as nationalist propaganda aimed at preserving the “Japanese spirit” among emigrants. It concludes that Sato appears fairly harmless and distinguishes the movement from sedition or incitement.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division distribution sheet
subfiles.to: War Department, State Department, and Commerce Department offices
subfiles.about: Lists offices to which the accompanying intelligence material could be circulated.
subfiles.summary: This administrative sheet enumerates military branches and civilian departments, including the State Department’s Far East office. It provides routing options for information, return, or further transmission.

subfiles.title: Japanese Propagandist
subfiles.from: James I. Muir, Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Hawaiian Department
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Transmits two intelligence reports about Teikichi Sato’s speeches in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Muir forwards reports dated March 9 and April 9 concerning Sato’s Honolulu and rural-island activities. He explains the religious significance of the mirror, sword, and jewel and notes that Sato departed Honolulu for the continental United States on April 7.

subfiles.title: Report on Teikichi Sato
subfiles.to: Office of the Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Hawaiian Department
subfiles.about: Reports Sato’s background, organizational affiliations, and nationalist-religious lectures in Honolulu.
subfiles.summary: The report describes Sato as an engineer, Christian leader, and officer of the Union for the Promotion of Japan, then outlines that organization’s religious and nationalist program. It recounts his lectures at McKinley High School, Mid-Pacific Institute, and the Nuuanu YMCA. Sato argued that Japan had a divinely ordained mission to lead Pacific civilization and urged local Japanese to preserve and transmit the Japanese national spirit.
keywords: Union for the Promotion of Japan

subfiles.title: Supplemental report on Dr. Sato’s island lectures
subfiles.to: Office of the Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Hawaiian Department
subfiles.about: Reports allegedly disloyal statements made by Sato to Japanese audiences outside Honolulu.
subfiles.summary: An informant claimed that Sato advocated “100% Japanism” and familiarity with the imperial mirror, sword, and jewel. At Ewa plantation he allegedly advised Japanese American soldiers not to fire at Japanese troops in a future war. The report adds that many local Japanese listeners were disgusted and left before he finished.

subfiles.title: Document file note: Japanese tankers in Hawaiian waters
subfiles.about: Cross-references a letter concerning Japanese tankers and suspected intelligence agents in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The note points to file 894.3511/158. It states that Japanese tankers were habitually observed in Hawaiian waters during maneuvers and Pan-Pacific gatherings and that “special visitors” aboard might be intelligence agents.

subfiles.title: Document file note: Japanese propaganda in Hawaiian schools
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report alleging that Japanese-language schools promoted loyalty to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The note refers readers to file 811a.42/16. It summarizes a statement attributed to the Japanese consul general that Hawaii’s Japanese-language schools fostered loyalty to Japan among Hawaiian-born Japanese.

subfiles.title: Two Letters Signed W. K. Lyhan
subfiles.from: James I. Muir, Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Hawaiian Department
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Evaluates two letters written by Kilsoo Han under the pseudonym W. K. Lyhan.
subfiles.summary: Muir identifies Lyhan as Kilsoo Han, a representative of the Sino-Korean People’s League, and reviews his shifting account of the sources behind his allegations. The report checks his claims about Japanese insurance and mutual-aid organizations and notes precautions concerning school propaganda. Although acknowledging that the allegations might be true, the office doubts their accuracy.

subfiles.title: Letter warning Alexander and Baldwin about Japanese insurance activity
subfiles.from: W. K. Lyhan, representative of the Sino-Korean People’s League
subfiles.to: Alexander and Baldwin, Ltd., Insurance Department
subfiles.about: Warns that a Japanese life-insurance company would promote Japanization and compete with Hawaiian insurers.
subfiles.summary: Lyhan alleges that the Japanese government planned to send the Nihkwa Life Insurance Company to Hawaii as part of a network influencing schools, cultural groups, and religious organizations. He links the plan to expatriation, racial solidarity in business, and Japanese shipping of Philippine sugar. He urges protective fair-competition legislation.

subfiles.title: Letter warning George M. Collins about Japanese educational propaganda
subfiles.from: W. K. Lyhan, confidential representative of the Sino-Korean People’s League
subfiles.to: George M. Collins, chairman of the school commissioners
subfiles.about: Alleges a Japanese government plan to distribute national-defense and cultural material in Hawaiian schools.
subfiles.summary: Lyhan claims that a Japanese interdepartmental conference approved projects for Japanese-language schools and Hawaii’s public schools. He attributes arrangements to Okada and quotes Setsuichi Aoki on systematic propaganda intended to make American children friendly to Japan. The letter warns that the program would obstruct the Americanization of Japanese Americans.

subfiles.title: Department of State receipt and routing stamps
subfiles.to: Division of Communications and Records; Under Secretary
subfiles.about: Records departmental receipt and internal routing of the preceding intelligence packet.
subfiles.summary: The page consists chiefly of State Department date and routing stamps. It shows processing on or around February 18–20, 1935.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division distribution sheet
subfiles.to: War Department, State Department, and Commerce Department offices
subfiles.about: Provides a distribution list for the copied Lyhan correspondence and intelligence assessment.
subfiles.summary: The form lists military branches and civilian departmental offices. Its check-box language allows the packet to be filed, returned, or sent onward.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Two Letters Signed W. K. Lyhan
subfiles.from: James I. Muir, Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Hawaiian Department
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Duplicates the assessment of Kilsoo Han’s two pseudonymous letters.
subfiles.summary: This degraded copy repeats Muir’s identification of W. K. Lyhan as Kilsoo Han and his account of Han’s sources and Korean nationalist commission. It also repeats the checks on insurance organizations and preparations to detect propaganda in schools. Muir again expresses doubt about the allegations’ accuracy.

subfiles.title: Duplicate letter on Japanese insurance activity
subfiles.about: Duplicates Lyhan’s warning about Japanese insurance, expatriation, and commercial competition.
subfiles.summary: The duplicate claims that a Japanese insurance enterprise would assist Japanization in Hawaii and work with education, cultural, Buddhist, and Shinto groups. It discusses expatriation figures, Japanese business practices, and Philippine sugar carriage. Lyhan recommends fair-competition legislation.

subfiles.title: Duplicate letter on Japanese educational propaganda
subfiles.about: Duplicates Lyhan’s allegations concerning Japanese material for public and language schools.
subfiles.summary: The copy alleges that Japanese agencies planned to distribute national-defense materials to Japanese schools and free reference materials to public schools. It quotes Japanese cultural officials and argues that the effort would undermine Americanization. The OCR is substantially degraded but the text parallels pages 15–16.

subfiles.title: John Doe memorandum on Japanese population, culture, and Hawaiian statehood
subfiles.about: Argues that Japanese demographic growth and cultural practices threatened American control and statehood in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The anonymous writer cites population figures, Japanese-language schools, education in Japan, festivals, expatriation, voting, and employment to portray Japanese residents as permanently loyal to Japan. The memorandum advocates fingerprinting, restricting Army employment of Japanese servants, and commission or district government instead of statehood. It includes quotations or clippings about Dr. Harry I. Kurisaki and Professor Kiyooka.

subfiles.title: Carps Flown on Boys’ Day
subfiles.about: Explains Japanese Boys’ Day customs observed in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The article describes carp streamers, samurai figures, gift exchanges, prayers, sake, and iris baths associated with the May 5 festival. It relates the carp to courage and to the legend of Empress Jingū’s expedition against Korea. Handwritten commentary questions whether Japanese Americans’ observance is compatible with Americanism.

subfiles.title: Training Ship of Japan Here
subfiles.about: Reports the Honolulu visit of the Japanese fisheries training ship Hakuyo Maru.
subfiles.summary: The Hakuyo Maru arrived from Dutch Harbor with cadets, officers, crew, a small cannery, and canned salmon and crab. Its cadets studied navigation, seamanship, fishing, and canning before a planned voyage to the Japanese-mandated Pacific islands. Captain Jinzo Nakagawa and cadet Iwame Torahike are identified in the caption.

subfiles.title: Japanese Students Will Visit Here
subfiles.about: Fragmentarily announces a visit by forty-eight Japanese students.
subfiles.summary: Only the headline and a few lines survive. The clipping states that forty-eight students from Japanese schools and colleges were scheduled to arrive for a brief one-day visit.

subfiles.title: Be Loyal to America, Consul Tells Delegates
subfiles.about: Reports a New Americans conference devoted to Japanese Americans’ citizenship and loyalty.
subfiles.summary: Japanese Consul General Kosaku Midzusawa, General Charles D. Herron, Commander John H. Buchanan, and other speakers urged delegates to be loyal Americans. Speakers expressed confidence in Japanese Americans while arguing against dual citizenship and in favor of expatriation from Japanese nationality. The article also lists conference organizers, island delegates, and social events.

subfiles.title: Lantern Festival Opens on Thursday
subfiles.about: Briefly announces O-Bon ceremonies and later Bon-Odori dances in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The notice describes three days of services at the Hompa Hongwanji and the belief that spirits of the dead return during O-Bon. It lists several Hawaiian communities where Bon-Odori dances would later be held.

subfiles.title: Japanese Here to Observe Ancient Lantern Festival
subfiles.about: Explains the religious rites, household practices, and folk dances of O-Bon in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Yamada describes temple services, graveyard visits, lanterns, offerings, sutra chanting, and the belief that ancestral spirits return for three days. He traces the observance to the arrival of Buddhism in Japan and discusses the Iwakuni and Becho forms of Bon-Odori popular in Hawaii. The article notes that the festival’s social and recreational aspects had partly displaced its religious meaning.

subfiles.title: Japanese Observing O-Bon
subfiles.about: Fragmentarily notes daily O-Bon services at the Hompa Hongwanji.
subfiles.summary: The surviving text identifies the Hompa Hongwanji on upper Fort Street as a center for services. It adds that Buddhist sects throughout Hawaii would observe the occasion.

subfiles.title: Japan Offering $12,000 Pay for American Propagandist
subfiles.from: Drew Pearson and Robert S. Allen
subfiles.about: Claims that Japan employed or subsidized American publicists and cultural organizations.
subfiles.summary: The column says the Japanese government was seeking a Washington journalist to replace a deceased propagandist and estimates Japanese propaganda spending in the United States at five million dollars annually. It identifies the Kokusai Bunka Shinkokai as a major cultural-propaganda organization and lists several paid advisers, press agents, and lecturers. Free travel for businesspeople and teachers is described as another instrument of influence.

subfiles.title: Home-rule resolution before Honolulu supervisors
subfiles.about: Reports a proposed congressional mandate permitting Hawaiian counties to adopt charters.
subfiles.summary: The clipping describes a resolution seeking county charters, plebiscites, taxing and bonding authority, and freedom from territorial legislative control. Wilfred C. Tsukiyama drafted the measure, and Supervisor Philip N. Sing introduced it.

subfiles.title: Ship Is Here With Scrap for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the Rio Novo’s Honolulu stop while carrying American scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Norwegian freighter arrived with 4,200 tons of scrap iron loaded in Florida and took on American fuel oil before continuing to Japan. The article lists its subsequent itinerary, ownership, home port, and master, Captain Einar Muller.

subfiles.title: Statehood Seen as Influence on Islands’ Loyalty
subfiles.about: Quotes Riley H. Allen on Japanese population and Hawaiian statehood.
subfiles.summary: Allen argues that Hawaii’s large Japanese population affected popular thinking about statehood but had no real bearing on the question. He also predicts that there would be no war with Japan during the current generation.

subfiles.title: U.S. Action on Aliens Is Doubted
subfiles.about: Discusses possible consequences for Japanese aliens after abrogation of the 1911 Japanese-American treaty.
subfiles.summary: The dispatch considers higher duties on Japanese goods and discriminatory state or local laws affecting Japanese residents. It notes that Japan could retaliate against Americans in Japan, China, and Manchukuo and quotes the treaty’s protections for residence, trade, property, and equal taxation. The article concludes that the treaty provisions had restrained official discrimination without eliminating racial friction.

subfiles.title: Keep That Money for Japanese Relief
subfiles.about: Objects to Hawaiian Japanese fundraising for Japan while local Japanese residents received public relief.
subfiles.summary: The correspondent complains that local Japanese sent money and trucks to aid Japan’s war in China. The writer contrasts those contributions with taxpayer support for hungry or sick Japanese residents in Hawaii.

subfiles.title: Britain Suggests Blockade Be Lifted
subfiles.about: Reports British pressure on Japan to end the blockade of the British concession at Tientsin.
subfiles.summary: The dispatch says Lord Halifax instructed Ambassador Sir Robert Craigie to seek an immediate end to the blockade. It connects the move with U.S. abrogation of the Japanese trade treaty and mentions anti-British demonstrations and food shortages in Tientsin.

subfiles.title: Japan Strengthens Ties with Axis
subfiles.about: Reports closer Japanese economic ties with the Rome-Berlin Axis.
subfiles.summary: The fragment states that Japan was materially strengthening its Axis ties. It refers to a new trade treaty with Germany as reinforcing economic relations.

subfiles.title: Canadians Jittery Over War, Fear They May Be Drawn In
subfiles.about: Examines anti-Japanese discrimination and Japanese Canadian responses during the Sino-Japanese War.
subfiles.summary: Peet reports boycotts, occupational restrictions, disenfranchisement, and a failed proposal to segregate Japanese residents and exclude them from fishing. An unnamed Vancouver merchant argues that Japanese Canadians sought fair treatment and that the second generation would make loyal citizens. The article also discusses Canadians’ fear that Britain might enter the Asian war and notes Chinese and Japanese passengers returning across the Pacific.

subfiles.title: Another Friend for Hawaii
subfiles.about: Condemns federal economic discrimination against Hawaiian sugar and demands equal treatment for Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The editorial calls Hawaii vital to Pacific defense and criticizes import policies favoring foreign sugar, especially Cuban sugar, over Hawaiian production. It argues that Hawaii is an integral American territory entitled to the same market treatment as the states. The piece frames trade barriers against Hawaii as a form of internal Balkanization.

subfiles.title: A Matter of Timing
subfiles.about: Interprets the timing and probable economic effect of U.S. abrogation of the 1911 treaty with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The editorial argues that the timing, shortly after a British setback in East Asia, signaled U.S. displeasure with Japan. It notes that the six-month notice was not intrinsically severe but would create economic pressure while Japan needed American trade and banking facilities to sustain war and reconstruction. The writer predicts that the action would influence Japanese policy during the following months.

subfiles.title: Boys’ Day Fete Friday
subfiles.about: Describes the Japanese Boys’ Day or Iris Festival and its symbols of courage and manhood.
subfiles.summary: Yamada explains the use of iris leaves and baths, carp streamers, and images of feudal heroes in Japanese homes. The carp’s endurance and calmness in death are compared with the expected courage of the samurai. The article notes that the customs continued in Hawaii, though less extensively than in Japan.

subfiles.title: 313 Will Get U.H. Degrees
subfiles.about: Announces University of Hawaii commencement totals and lists degree recipients.
subfiles.summary: The article reports that 313 students would receive bachelor’s degrees at the university’s twenty-eighth commencement, alongside graduate degrees, five-year diplomas, and public-health nursing certificates. Pages 43–44 reproduce long, partially duplicated lists of Bachelor of Arts, Bachelor of Science, and Bachelor of Education recipients. The Bachelor of Education list is cut off at the end of page 44.
